content: The measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine, or the combined measles, mumps, rubella, and varicella (MMRV) vaccine, contains a specific number of infectious units per dose (≥1000 PFU or CCID50). Tetanus booster vaccines are essential for adolescents and adults to maintain high antibody levels, which can persist for decades. Administering booster doses during pre-adolescence and adolescence is programmatically feasible and aligns with the human papillomavirus (HPV) immunization schedule. For HIV prevention in adolescents, antiretroviral drugs should be used for both treatment and prevention. HIV testing services, linked to prevention, treatment, and care, should be accessible to adolescents in all settings, particularly for key populations. Adolescents living with HIV should receive counseling on the benefits and risks of disclosing their HIV status and be supported in deciding if, when, how, and to whom they disclose this information. In generalized HIV epidemics, testing services should be offered to all adolescents, while in concentrated epidemics, services should be accessible to adolescents in low-level and concentrated epidemic areas. Community-based approaches can improve treatment adherence and retention in care for adolescents living with HIV. Comprehensive condom and lubricant programs are critical, as adolescents, especially those from key populations, may face power imbalances in sexual relationships that limit their ability to use condoms. Peer-led and outreach approaches can help distribute condoms and lubricants, increase knowledge, and empower adolescents to use them correctly and consistently. Adolescent-friendly health services should be implemented in HIV care to improve engagement and outcomes. Trained lay providers can distribute antiretroviral therapy (ART) to adolescents, and ART should be initiated in all adolescents living with HIV, regardless of clinical stage or CD4 count, with priority given to those with advanced disease or low CD4 counts. Voluntary medical male circumcision is recommended for HIV prevention in countries with high HIV prevalence and low rates of male circumcision, particularly targeting adolescents and young men. Sexual and reproductive health services, including contraceptive information and services, should be provided to adolescents without requiring parental or guardian authorization. Adolescents may avoid health services if they believe parental permission is mandatory, increasing the risk of unsafe abortion. HPV vaccination does not replace cervical cancer screening, and screening programs should be developed or strengthened in countries where the vaccine is introduced. The recommended target group for HPV vaccination is girls aged 9–13 years, including those living with HIV. Pregnant women and adolescents living with HIV should receive appropriate treatment and care to prevent mother-to-child transmission of HIV. Many women, particularly adolescents, have inadequate access to antenatal care and prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) services. Young individuals considering surgical sterilization should be counseled on its permanence and the availability of alternative long-term, effective methods. Studies show that up to 20% of women sterilized at a young age later regret the decision, with young age being a strong predictor of regret. Similarly, young men undergoing vasectomy are more likely to seek reversal compared to older men. Adolescents can generally use depot medroxyprogesterone acetate (DMPA) as a contraceptive method. Combined hormonal contraceptives (CHCs) may decrease bone mineral density (BMD) in adolescents, particularly with very low-dose formulations, but have little to no effect on BMD in premenopausal women. Sexuality education programs should provide scientifically accurate and comprehensive information on contraceptive use and acquisition. Safe abortion information and services should be provided according to WHO guidelines. For physical activity, children and adolescents aged 5–17 years should engage in at least 60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity daily, with additional health benefits from exceeding this amount. Most activity should be aerobic, with vigorous-intensity activities, including muscle and bone strengthening, incorporated at least three times per week. To promote mental health, non-specialized healthcare facilities should collaborate with schools to provide life skills education. Suicide prevention programs in schools, including mental health awareness and skills training, can reduce suicide attempts and deaths among adolescents. WHO recommends reducing free sugar intake to less than 10% of total energy intake, with further reduction to below 5% suggested for additional health benefits. Pregnant women should receive counseling on healthy eating and physical activity to prevent excessive weight gain. In undernourished populations, nutrition education and balanced energy-protein dietary supplementation are recommended to reduce risks of low birth weight and stillbirths. High-protein supplementation is not recommended. Daily iron and folic acid supplementation is advised to prevent maternal anemia and improve neonatal outcomes. Calcium supplementation is recommended in populations with low calcium intake to reduce pre-eclampsia risk. Vitamin A supplementation is recommended only in areas with severe deficiency to prevent night blindness. Zinc supplementation during pregnancy is recommended only in the context of rigorous research. Multiple micronutrient supplementation is not recommended as an alternative to standard iron and folic acid supplementation. Vitamin B6, vitamin E, vitamin C, and vitamin D supplementation are not recommended for improving maternal and perinatal outcomes. Pregnant women with high caffeine intake should reduce consumption to lower the risk of pregnancy loss and low birth weight. Birth preparedness and complication readiness interventions are recommended to increase the use of skilled care at birth and timely facility care for complications. Male involvement during pregnancy, childbirth, and postpartum is encouraged to support women’s self-care and improve maternal and newborn health outcomes, provided it respects women’s autonomy and decision-making. Dialogue with traditional birth attendants (TBAs) and communities is recommended to define alternative roles for TBAs, recognizing their importance in supporting maternal and newborn health. Lay health workers, including trained TBAs, can promote maternal and newborn health behaviors and services, provide social support during labor, and administer interventions like misoprostol to prevent postpartum hemorrhage. Culturally appropriate maternity care should be defined through ongoing dialogue with communities, ensuring women’s voices are included. Continuous companionship during labor and birth is recommended to improve women’s satisfaction with care.
